extracted.intended_audience: general readers, mathematicians, philosophers, psychologists, and neuroscientists interested in the aesthetics of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the properties, criteria and standards discussed for judging the aesthetic value of mathematical results, proofs, theories, and objects as presented in the Wikipedia article 'Mathematical beauty'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardy's three aesthetic qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful result (including its proof) possesses three 'purely aesthetic qualities': inevitability, unexpectedness, and economy. Hardy particularly excluded enumeration of cases as 'one of the duller forms of mathematical argument'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy's triad is often cited as a concise checklist: does the result/proof feel inevitable once seen, yet was it unexpected; is it economical (concise, not wasteful in steps or assumptions)? The article also notes disagreement about whether unexpectedness is sufficient for beauty (see Rota).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and brevity of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that are short and simple are customarily thought beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians often search for simpler proofs of known results because the first proof can often be improved; the Pythagorean theorem is cited as having hundreds of proofs. Short, simple proofs are prized as giving clarity and insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of case enumeration / heavy computer checking (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Results that are logically correct but rely on laborious calculations or consideration of many cases (e.g., heavy case enumeration or extensive computer checking) are not usually considered beautiful and may be called 'ugly' or 'clumsy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Appel–Haken proof of the four-colour theorem is given as an example: reliance on checking over a thousand cases and computer verification led many to regard it as lacking beauty because it gave no insight. Paul Erdős explicitly said such a proof was 'not beautiful'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification / linking of disparate concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical expressions or theorems that tie together important or seemingly unrelated constants, objects, or ideas are often experienced as beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euler's identity (e^(iπ) + 1 = 0) is cited as beautiful because it connects five fundamental constants (e, i, π, 1, 0) and basic symbols; Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares is another historical example. Unity and unexpected connections are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order, symmetry, and definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle identified order, symmetry and definiteness as chief forms of beauty, and these have been invoked as properties conducive to mathematical beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These classical aesthetic qualities manifest in mathematical structures and arguments (e.g., symmetry in groups, regular solids) and are presented as enduring criteria from philosophical tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity and austerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical beauty is characterized by purity and austerity — a 'cold and austere' beauty without ornamentation, according to Bertrand Russell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Russell's formulation emphasizes an aesthetic appreciation for mathematical 'purity' (e.g., elegant minimal assumptions or formulations) akin to sculptural rather than sensory art-forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance (and its relation to beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors identify mathematical elegance with mathematical beauty; others distinguish elegance as a separate aesthetic value, possibly limited to the form of exposition rather than substantive beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes a spectrum of views: elegance may describe succinct, graceful exposition, while beauty might be a broader judgment tied to depth, unity, or insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness (contested as a sufficient condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpectedness — the surprising quality of a result — is commonly cited as part of mathematical beauty (Hardy), but some (e.g., Gian‑Carlo Rota) argue that unexpectedness alone is not sufficient for beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rota gives counterexamples of surprising theorems not deemed beautiful; responses note that particular realizations or especially explicit/insightful presentations of surprising facts can be beautiful (Monastyrsky on Milnor's construction). This highlights the subjective and context-dependent nature of 'unexpectedness'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth of a result or proof — how many layers of meaning, consequences, or nontrivial ideas it contains — is often linked to perceptions of mathematical beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depth is invoked alongside abstractness, purity and simplicity as properties that can contribute to beauty; deep constructions or realizations that reveal structure are frequently praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstractness (the level of conceptual abstraction) is often associated with mathematical beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mathematics is highly abstract, beauty is experienced in contemplating abstract ideas (not just sensory objects); this abstractness may restrict appreciation to those with the requisite training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic compressibility / low Kolmogorov complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Schmidhuber's information‑theory model: among subjectively comparable objects, the most beautiful are those with short algorithmic descriptions (low Kolmogorov complexity) relative to what the observer already knows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This account connects beauty to compressibility and predictability: 'interestingness' corresponds to compression progress (the first derivative of perceived beauty) when an observer learns new regularities. The model is explicitly observer‑dependent and links aesthetic pleasure to information‑theoretic notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualisability and determinism as influences on beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a scientific theory (expressed mathematically) is visualisable or deterministic can influence whether it is seen as beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that mathematical statements of scientific theories (e.g., Maxwell's equations, general relativity) are often called beautiful; additional non-mathematical features (visualisability, determinism) may enhance aesthetic judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of independent proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of many different, independent proofs of a theorem is often regarded as a sign of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Pythagorean theorem (hundreds of proofs) and quadratic reciprocity (many proofs, Gauss produced multiple proofs). Multiple proofs can reveal varied insights and strengthen perceptions of inevitability and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual proofs / 'proofs without words'
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual proofs and 'proofs without words' are generally thought to be beautiful because they provide immediate, often pictorial insight into why a result holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The illustrated Pythagorean theorem and pictured proof that the sum of odd numbers up to 2^n − 1 is a perfect square are cited; such proofs emphasize immediacy and clarity of understanding.
